prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice atomic clocks that reach a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I did not rank B029 in my opening ballot, and I want to say so plainly: my first place went to the cavity method for random constraint-satisfaction problems (B039), which lies close to my own field. Having read the eight ballots, I move to B029 as the preferred single-achievement prize because the colleagues' case is the strongest that the shortlist offers on the criteria that matter. Six of eight members ranked it and two put it first, and the arguments are independent of one another: a single, well-defined idea (magic-wavelength trapping, which removes Doppler and recoil limits while keeping large atom numbers), a clean experimental realisation by a second group that pushed strontium clocks to 10^-18, independent reproduction at several national laboratories, and consequences beyond the instrument itself (tests of constancy of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy, many-body effects in clocks). Katori and Ye are the two names every colleague who proposed laureates chose, so attribution is unusually uncontested for a prize of this kind. It is a measurement-based discovery with a stable interpretation, which I regard as a better basis for an award than a candidate whose standing depends on how one weighs a field that is still moving.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision timekeeping has already been honoured twice in recent decades, for the frequency comb in 2005 (Hall and Hansch) and for the control of single trapped ions in 2012 (Wineland and Haroche), and the lattice clock reads out through the comb and borrows ion-clock ideas. A sceptical reader can call this an incremental continuation. Second, I am a statistical physicist and not a metrologist, so I cannot independently judge how much of the 10^-18 result belongs to the lattice concept itself and how much to laser stabilisation and cavity engineering that other groups also contributed (for example the Paris, PTB and NIST clock groups). Third, the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, and I do not want practical expectation to be mistaken for scientific merit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B029 first because the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil limits while retaining large atom numbers, and he notes confirmation across many laboratories and a stable interpretation, while flagging the Hall/JILA environment as a possible perceived conflict.
responses.response: I accept the physical argument and it is what moved me, since the concept is simple and the confirmation is broad. I would qualify it in one respect: independent confirmation of the performance is not the same as independent confirmation of the credit, and Kroll's own note about Ye's long association with the Hall environment is a reason for the committee to keep the citation tied to the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, not to frequency-comb or spectroscopy work already honoured in 2005. I have no relationship to any of the people involved that would make the point personal.

responses.point: Lindroth places B029 first, calls the idea original and clean with transparent atomic physics, and stresses that JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST have all confirmed 1e-18 performance, while asking whether the prize should be paired with earlier comb work or blurred by ion clocks.
responses.response: I agree that the multi-laboratory confirmation is the decisive point, and her worry about blurring is the right one. Where I differ slightly is on pairing: I would not add a second achievement to dilute the citation, because the credited set for a second part would push the union past three people and force a weaker partner. A narrow two-name citation on the lattice clock answers her concern about overlap with the ion-clock prize better than a composite would.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery (B012) first, arguing that the 2013 prize honoured only the theory, that the discovery is beyond doubt and mature, and that credit should go to the founders and leaders of ATLAS and CMS.
responses.response: I agree that the importance of the discovery is beyond doubt and that I would not oppose it as a topic; I ranked it seventh and that is a statement about attribution, not about merit. My serious reservation is that Danielsson's own assessment concedes that the three-person allocation of Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is imperfect and rests on general knowledge, not on verified roles. A prize for a result produced by two collaborations of several thousand people is only as strong as its credited names, and the lattice clock does not have that weakness. If the committee finds a defensible rule for crediting the experiments, I would revisit it, but I cannot support it on the present evidence.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the gamma-ray burst afterglow discovery (B013) first and IceCube neutrino astronomy with a single credited name (B037) second, arguing that both are concrete observations that opened a field, and he ranks B029 third.
responses.response: I respect the observational case, but I disagree with crediting IceCube to one person when, as Pearce himself notes, the result is the work of a large collaboration and a decades-long effort including AMANDA and earlier neutrino-telescope pioneers. He also states that source identification beyond the diffuse flux is statistically modest and awaits independent confirmation, which makes the maturity weaker than for B029. For B013 I cannot evaluate the weight of the X-ray discovery against the optical and redshift follow-up and would want the astrophysicists to settle whether the credited trio really covers the decisive contributors, since he notes that van Paradijs is absent.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory (B035) first, as the first controllable non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, but concedes that Metzner is omitted from the credited names and that single-site DMFT has limited reliability when nonlocal correlations are strong.
responses.response: As a theorist I am sympathetic to the conceptual weight of DMFT, and the infinite-dimension limit is a beautiful piece of statistical physics. But the omission of Metzner that Eriksson himself flags, together with the limits of the single-site approximation, leaves the attribution and the claim of general validity less secure than a result that has been measured in several laboratories. I would put it behind B029 for those reasons, not because of its originality.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-quantum-system control, or as a continuation of them.
How the contributions of other lattice-clock groups (for example the Paris, PTB and NIST groups) weigh against the credited pair, which I cannot judge from the supplied record.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, which I think should not drive the decision but which colleagues may weigh differently.

My own top-ranked B039 (Mezard and Zecchina) was supported by no other member; I cannot tell whether that reflects a real weakness in its experimental or physical standing, or that colleagues outside statistical physics did not weigh its significance, and the 2021 recognition of disordered systems may overlap with its cavity-method foundations.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented co-authors and supervisors (Fulde, Gustavsson, Wilkinson, Einarsson, Candelier, Pumir, Meibohm) are not among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate, and I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited individuals. My own first-ranked candidate, B039, is near my field of statistical physics of disordered systems, which is an intellectual proximity, not a personal tie.
